questions.question: You are deploying Azure AI capabilities for an enterprise app and need a single endpoint and key that authorise calls to Vision, Language, Speech and Translator with consolidated billing. Which resource type should you create?
options: Four separate single-service resources, one per API, sharing a resource group
An Azure API Management gateway placed in front of four single-service resources
A multi-service Azure AI services resource exposing one shared endpoint and key
An Azure AI Foundry hub workspace used on its own as the inference endpoint
questions.explanation: A multi-service Azure AI services resource exposes a single endpoint and key that authorise Vision, Language, Speech, Translator and other Azure AI APIs, and rolls all usage onto one bill. Provisioning a separate single-service resource per API leaves you managing a distinct endpoint and key for each one and produces a separate line item per service. An API Management gateway can unify routing in front of those resources, but the single-service resources still exist, are still billed individually and still each have their own key — APIM adds a façade rather than consolidating the underlying service. An Azure AI Foundry hub organises projects, models, connections and governance for AI workloads; it is not the resource that serves Vision/Language/Speech/Translator inference traffic.

questions.question: Your team must rotate the access keys on a production Azure AI Language resource without interrupting client traffic that is already in flight. Which sequence is recommended?
options: Regenerate the currently unused key, move all clients to it, then rotate the other
Regenerate both key1 and key2 simultaneously and redeploy every client in parallel
Regenerate the key clients are actively using and let them reconnect to the new value
Delete the resource and recreate it so brand-new keys are issued for both slots
questions.explanation: Azure AI resources expose two keys precisely so you can rotate with zero downtime: regenerate the key no client is currently using, migrate every client to that freshly rotated key, then regenerate the other. Regenerating both keys at once invalidates every live connection until all clients have been redeployed with new credentials, creating an authentication-error window. Regenerating the key clients are actively using breaks their in-flight calls immediately because that key value is invalidated the moment the regenerate operation completes. Deleting and recreating the resource also forces a brand-new resource ID and endpoint, so every client must be reconfigured for both the keys and the URL — that is a re-provision, not a key rotation.

questions.question: A retailer wants to detect and locate their own product SKUs inside shelf photographs using a small set of labelled images and a no-code training portal. Which Azure service fits best?
options: Azure AI Vision Image Analysis 4.0 relying on its built-in generic object tagging
Azure AI Document Intelligence with a custom-trained field-extraction model
Azure AI Video Indexer with a custom-trained brand-and-object model applied to stills
An Azure AI Custom Vision object-detection project trained on the labelled images
questions.explanation: Azure AI Custom Vision lets you upload a small set of labelled images in a no-code portal and train an object-detection model that returns bounding boxes for your own product SKUs. Image Analysis 4.0 recognises only generic objects from Microsoft's prebuilt taxonomy — it cannot be taught new SKU classes from labelled examples. Document Intelligence extracts key-value fields from forms and documents and has no concept of locating products within a natural-scene shelf photo. Video Indexer is built for video timelines; while it does support custom brand insights, those run over video frames and faces/audio, not still product photographs, so it is the wrong modality for a SKU detector trained on labelled stills.

questions.question: The prebuilt invoice model in Azure AI Document Intelligence is missing several vendor-specific fields that your finance team needs extracted automatically. What should you do next?
options: Switch the prebuilt invoice model to its receipt-extraction variant for the missing fields
Label a few vendor-specific documents and train a custom extraction model
Run the Read OCR model and parse the missing fields with regular expressions
Compose the prebuilt invoice model together with the prebuilt receipt model
questions.explanation: When a prebuilt model omits fields you need, you label a small set of representative documents in Document Intelligence Studio and train a custom extraction model that learns those vendor-specific fields and reuses the prebuilt structure. The prebuilt invoice model has no 'receipt variant' to switch to — invoice and receipt are separate prebuilt models with different schemas, and the receipt one extracts merchant/total/items, not vendor-specific invoice fields. Running Read OCR followed by regex parsing throws away the layout and key-value structure the service already understands, making extraction brittle and high-maintenance. Model composition combines several custom models behind one endpoint so an incoming document can be routed to the right one; it does not add new fields to a prebuilt model.

questions.question: Your chatbot must classify each user utterance into an intent and extract entities such as dates and locations from it. Which Azure AI Language feature should you use?
options: Custom named entity recognition (custom NER) configured on its own
Sentiment analysis with opinion mining enabled on each utterance
Conversational language understanding (CLU) with a trained model
An orchestration workflow that routes utterances to other projects
questions.explanation: Conversational language understanding (CLU), the successor to LUIS, is purpose-built to predict an intent and extract entities from each utterance within a single trained model. Custom NER extracts named entities only and has no concept of intents, so it cannot classify the utterance itself. Sentiment analysis with opinion mining returns sentiment polarity and aspect-level opinions; it does not learn intents or extract date/location entities. An orchestration workflow connects and routes between an underlying CLU project, custom question answering and other projects — it relies on a CLU project to do the intent-and-entity work rather than performing that classification itself.

questions.question: A studio wants Azure to speak marketing copy in a voice that reproduces a specific brand spokesperson, built from professional studio recordings of that person. Which capability is required?
options: Custom Neural Voice trained on the spokesperson's studio recordings
A prebuilt neural voice chosen from the standard text-to-speech catalogue
Personal Voice, the instant zero-shot voice-cloning capability
An SSML voice style and role applied to a standard neural voice
questions.explanation: Azure Custom Neural Voice (the Professional tier) trains a synthetic voice from professional studio recordings of a real, consented speaker so it reproduces that spokesperson's identity, and is gated by Microsoft's Limited Access programme to prevent misuse. A prebuilt catalogue voice is a generic Microsoft-trained speaker; it has its own identity and cannot match a named brand spokesperson. Personal Voice also clones a voice, but it is the zero-shot, consumer-oriented option built from a very short sample — not the studio-trained professional brand voice the scenario describes. SSML voice styles and roles only adjust the expression, emotion or role of an existing voice; they cannot create a new speaker identity.

questions.question: You want an Azure OpenAI chat deployment to answer questions using your own private PDF policy documents, kept up to date with each release. Which pattern is recommended?
options: Fine-tune the GPT model on the PDF text so it memorises the policy content
Paste the entire text of every policy PDF into the system prompt on each call
Raise the deployment's context window and stream all PDFs in with each request
Index the PDFs in Azure AI Search and query them via the On Your Data feature
questions.explanation: The recommended Retrieval-Augmented Generation pattern is to chunk and embed the PDFs into an Azure AI Search index, then point the Azure OpenAI 'On Your Data' feature at that index so each query retrieves only the relevant passages. Fine-tuning bakes knowledge into model weights at training time — it teaches style and format rather than fresh facts, and re-running it on every release is slow, costly and still leaves the deployment stale between runs. Pasting every PDF into the system prompt burns tokens, raises latency and cost, and grounds nothing in retrieval. Simply enlarging the context window to fit all PDFs has the same token-cost and latency problem and still degrades accuracy as the document set grows — only indexed retrieval scales and stays current as policies change.

questions.question: By default, every Azure OpenAI deployment screens prompts and completions for harmful content across categories such as hate, violence, self-harm and sexual content. Which capability provides those built-in filters?
options: Microsoft Defender for Cloud AI workload threat-protection rules
Azure AI Content Safety filters integrated into the deployment
Azure Policy initiatives scoped to generative AI resources
Microsoft Purview sensitivity labels applied to the model output
questions.explanation: Azure OpenAI deployments include Azure AI Content Safety filters by default; they score every prompt and completion for hate, violence, self-harm and sexual content against severity thresholds, and also provide Prompt Shields and protected-material detection. Microsoft Defender for Cloud — including its AI threat-protection plan — monitors deployment-level posture and flags attacks against the resource, but it does not perform inline classification of the content of each completion. Azure Policy enforces how Azure resources are configured (region, SKU, tagging), not what text a user sends through them. Microsoft Purview sensitivity labels classify and protect data assets for governance and DLP; they do not moderate harmful content in model request/response traffic.

questions.question: Your assistant must call live external APIs (weather, inventory) during a chat turn and weave the results back into its reply. Which Azure OpenAI capability orchestrates that pattern?
options: Fine-tune the model on transcripts of previous real API responses
Embed the entire API reference documentation into every system prompt
Function (tool) calling, with a tools schema supplied in the request
Switch the deployment to the Assistants API code-interpreter tool
questions.explanation: Function (tool) calling lets the model emit a structured JSON call matching a tools schema you define in the request; your application then runs the real weather or inventory API and returns the result, which the model weaves into its reply. Fine-tuning on past transcripts bakes in stale snapshots of past responses and never invokes a live API at run time. Embedding API reference docs in the prompt only describes the APIs to the model — it cannot invoke them and consumes tokens for context the model cannot act on. The Assistants API code-interpreter tool runs sandboxed Python for data analysis and visualisation, not arbitrary external HTTP API calls, so it is not the orchestrator for this pattern.

questions.question: You add a 1,536-dimension embedding produced by Azure OpenAI text-embedding-ada-002 to each chunk in an Azure AI Search index so it can be retrieved by vector similarity. How should that field be defined?
options: Collection(Edm.Single) with a dimensions value and a vector profile
Collection(Edm.Double) marked searchable with the standard text analyzer
Edm.String set as both searchable and filterable for similarity queries
A complex field wrapping 1,536 numeric sub-fields, one per dimension
questions.explanation: A vector field in Azure AI Search is typed as Collection(Edm.Single) — a single-precision float array — and must declare a `dimensions` value (1536 here) plus a vector search profile that selects an algorithm such as HNSW. Collection(Edm.Double) is not a valid vector element type and cannot accept a dimensions property; a text analyzer is meaningless for numeric vectors anyway. Edm.String holds keyword text for full-text search and cannot back vector similarity, which compares float arrays. A complex type groups named sub-fields for structured objects and cannot be queried as a single embedding vector — the vector ranking algorithms operate on a single typed array, not on object trees.

questions.question: An Azure OpenAI chat application is being moved to production. Security requires that no API key be stored in the app, and that calls be authorized by the application's own Azure identity instead. Which approach should you implement?
options: Grant a managed identity the Cognitive Services OpenAI User role and call with Entra tokens
Store key1 in Azure Key Vault and have the app fetch it at startup with a connection string
Inject key2 from the release pipeline into an environment variable read by the app at boot
Front the resource with Azure API Management and forward a subscription key on each call
questions.explanation: Granting the app's managed identity the Cognitive Services OpenAI User role and acquiring Microsoft Entra tokens removes keys entirely and authorizes calls by the app's own identity, which is the requirement. Fetching key1 from Azure Key Vault still relies on a key — the Azure OpenAI resource is authenticated by the key, not by the app's identity, and the app must hold a vault-access secret too. Injecting key2 as an environment variable both stores a key inside the runtime environment and exposes it to anyone who can read the process or pipeline logs. Placing Azure API Management in front authorizes the caller against the gateway with a subscription key, but APIM still has to authenticate to the Azure OpenAI resource downstream — typically with a key — so the requirement to eliminate keys is not met.

questions.question: A multilingual support team must translate inbound chat messages into English in real time, automatically detecting the source language of each message without it being specified. Which Azure AI service capability handles this?
options: Azure AI Language key phrase extraction passed to a separately built translation step
Azure AI Speech speech translation configured for text-to-text language conversion
Azure AI Language abstractive summarization with the target language set to English
Azure AI Translator text translation, which auto-detects the source language by default
questions.explanation: Azure AI Translator's text translation API detects the source language automatically when the 'from' parameter is omitted and returns the translated text in the requested target language, which fits real-time chat translation. Key phrase extraction surfaces salient terms from text; it does not translate, so an extra translation step would still be required. Speech translation operates on spoken audio input and produces translated speech or text from audio — it is the wrong modality for typed chat messages. Summarization condenses text into a shorter form; it does not translate between languages even when a target language parameter is supplied.

questions.question: A media archive needs to make spoken dialogue in thousands of recorded video files searchable, producing time-stamped transcripts plus detected topics and faces. Which Azure service is purpose-built for this?
options: Azure AI Vision Image Analysis applied frame-by-frame to keyframes extracted from each clip
Azure AI Speech batch transcription paired with a separately built Azure AI Search index
Azure AI Video Indexer, producing transcripts, topics, faces and a searchable timeline
Azure AI Document Intelligence Read model applied to subtitle sidecar files for each video
questions.explanation: Azure AI Video Indexer analyses audio and video together to produce time-stamped transcripts, topic detection, face detection and a searchable index across many files — exactly the archive scenario. Image Analysis on exported stills loses the audio track entirely and therefore cannot transcribe dialogue. Speech batch transcription returns text but no video-level insights such as faces or topics, so you would still need to rebuild face detection, topic extraction and the search index that Video Indexer already provides out of the box. The Document Intelligence Read model performs OCR on documents and depends on subtitle sidecar files that may not exist for raw recordings — and even when they do, it produces no faces or topic insights.

questions.question: You build an Azure AI Search index over support PDFs and want each document enriched with key phrases and detected language as it is ingested, with no custom code. Which Azure AI Search component performs this enrichment during indexing?
options: A scoring profile that boosts documents which contain the extracted key phrases at query time
A skillset of built-in cognitive skills run by the indexer to enrich documents on ingestion
A synonym map that expands query terms to language variants found across the indexed documents
A semantic ranker configuration applied to the index that reorders top results by relevance
questions.explanation: A skillset composed of built-in cognitive skills (key phrase extraction, language detection, OCR, entity recognition) runs inside the indexer pipeline and writes enriched fields with no custom code. A scoring profile only adjusts ranking weights at query time and cannot extract key phrases or detect a document's language during ingestion. A synonym map expands query terms before matching; it does not enrich indexed documents and does not run at ingestion time. The semantic ranker re-orders results at query time using language understanding over already-indexed fields and therefore performs no ingestion-time enrichment.

questions.question: A bank's Azure OpenAI assistant must never reveal another customer's data even if a user crafts an input designed to override the system instructions. Which Azure AI Content Safety capability is designed to detect that class of attack?
options: Protected material detection, which flags known copyrighted text in completions
Prompt Shields, which detect jailbreak and indirect prompt-injection attempts in inputs
Groundedness detection, which checks whether a completion is supported by source data
Severity-based category filters, which score outputs for hate, violence and self-harm
questions.explanation: Prompt Shields in Azure AI Content Safety are built to detect jailbreak attacks and indirect prompt-injection attempts that try to override system instructions, matching the described threat. Protected material detection flags known copyrighted text appearing in completions, which is a different content-risk class — it does not analyse user inputs for instruction-override attempts. Groundedness detection checks whether a response is supported by provided source data, which addresses hallucination rather than malicious input. Severity-based category filters score harmful-content categories such as hate and violence, not attempted manipulation of the system prompt.

questions.question: You must extract entities like 'policy number' and 'claim ID' that are specific to your insurer's documents and do not exist in the prebuilt entity categories of Azure AI Language. Which feature should you use?
options: Prebuilt named entity recognition (NER) filtered to the Quantity and Number categories
Personally identifiable information (PII) detection with the redaction option enabled
Entity linking, which associates recognized entities with Wikipedia knowledge-base IDs
Custom named entity recognition (custom NER) trained on your labelled documents
questions.explanation: Custom NER lets you label your own documents and train a model to extract domain-specific entities such as policy number and claim ID that prebuilt categories do not cover. Prebuilt NER recognizes only Microsoft's fixed category set and cannot learn insurer-specific fields — filtering to Quantity or Number returns generic numeric spans, not labelled policy numbers or claim IDs. PII detection finds and can redact personal data types (names, emails, SSNs), not arbitrary custom business identifiers. Entity linking disambiguates already-recognized entities against a public knowledge base (Wikipedia/Wikidata) and does not extract new custom entity types.
